title: Wisdom of Solomon
subtitle: a Greek-speaking Jew, in Solomon's voice, on justice, the soul, Wisdom and the God who rescued Israel from Egypt
lead: The Wisdom of Solomon is a Jewish book written in Greek, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in the century or so before Jesus or in his own lifetime. It never names its author. From chapter 7 on, the speaker talks as King Solomon, who asked God for wisdom (1 Kings 3:5–15), but the old copies already call it the "Wisdom of Solomon" only by its title, and from the early church on many readers have known that Solomon did not write it.

It has three movements. Chapters 1–5 call the rulers of the earth to love righteousness, let the ungodly speak their creed, "Life is short for us" (2:1), and show their plot against a righteous man, then promise that "the souls of the righteous are in God's hand" (3:1) and stage a judgment where the ungodly see him vindicated. Chapters 6–9 are Solomon's praise of Wisdom, the radiance of God's eternal light, and his prayer for her. Chapters 10–19 trace Wisdom through history from Adam to Moses and then, speaking straight to God, retell the Exodus as a set of contrasts: the things that punished Egypt helped Israel.

The Catholic Church and the Orthodox churches read it in their Old Testament. Anglicans and Lutherans place it among the Apocrypha, books read for example of life; most other Protestants and Judaism do not count it as Scripture. Every Christian tradition has read it closely, because the New Testament seems to know it: Hebrews 1:3, Romans 1 and 9, Ephesians 6 and 2 Corinthians 5 share words and images with it, two of them words that the Greek Old Testament uses only in this book.
facts: The Catholic Church (Trent, 1546) and the Eastern Orthodox churches (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose 81-book Bible counts it among the books of Solomon as Tebäb, "Wisdom" (Cowley, 1974). Among the Apocrypha for Anglicans (Article VI names "the Book of Wisdom") and Lutherans. Not Scripture for Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches, or for Judaism.

Unknown. The book speaks as Solomon in 7:1–9:18 but never names him. The Muratorian Fragment (a list Metzger dates to about 170) says it was written "by the friends of Solomon in his honour"; Jerome reports that some early writers credited it to Philo of Alexandria. The Catholic and Jewish Encyclopedias, Oesterley and the New American Bible's introduction all think of a Greek-speaking Jew, most likely of Alexandria; they differ on whether one writer or two wrote the two halves.

Unknown, and debated: proposals run from the reign of Ptolemy IV (221–204 BC; Gigot) to the reign of the emperor Caligula (AD 37–41; Winston) or just after it (AD 41–44; Goodrick). The Jewish Encyclopedia puts it about the middle of the first century BC, and the New American Bible's introduction "about fifty years before the coming of Christ." It quotes the Greek of Isaiah and of Job, so it is later than those translations.

No story setting: a speech to "you who judge the earth" (1:1) and to kings (6:1), spoken from 7:1 by a king in Jerusalem who was told to build the Temple (9:7–8). The last chapters look back on Egypt and the Exodus.
Most likely Alexandria in Egypt, the largest Greek-speaking Jewish city of the time: the book's Greek, its learning, its attack on Egyptian animal worship and its long look at Egypt all point there.

Greek. Jerome wrote that it "was never among the Hebrews, the very style of which reeks of Greek eloquence" (Edgecomb's translation). Gigot (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1912) reports that some proposed a Hebrew original, but that "it has been felt that not Hebrew but Greek was the original language."

Greek, in Codex Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus (300s–400s AD), which title it "Wisdom of Solomon," with Codex Ephraemi for parts of it; then later Greek copies and early translations, among them the Latin of the Vulgate, which the Douay-Rheims translates.

Poetry in the parallel lines of Hebrew verse, written in polished Greek: a call to rulers to love justice (1–6), a speech in Solomon's voice in praise of Wisdom with his prayer (7–9), and a retelling of Israel's history and the Exodus, addressed to God, with a long attack on idols (10–19).
authorship: The speaker of 7:1–9:18 is a king, "a mortal, the equal of everyone," who prayed for wisdom, was chosen to rule God's people and was told to build the Temple (7:7; 9:7–8). That is Solomon, though the book never writes his name. The Greek codices title it "Wisdom of Solomon" (Swete's note at 1:1).

Many early writers simply quoted it as Solomon's or as "the Wisdom of Solomon." Others doubted it from the start. The Muratorian Fragment, a list Metzger dates to about 170, has the Wisdom "written by the friends of Solomon in his honour" (in Metzger's translation); S. P. Tregelles suggested that the Latin translator misread a Greek "by Philo" as "by friends." Jerome (about 398) called it a "falsely ascribed work" and reported that some ancient writers held it to be Philo's. Augustine wrote that it had been customary to ascribe it to Solomon, but that "the more learned have no doubt that they are not his," and that the church, "especially the Western," had received it into authority (City of God 17.20).

Luther's preface (1534) says the book has long been disputed, that it is called Solomon's because it is written in his name and person, and that some hold Philo to be its master; he praised it all the same as worth reading.

Gigot (Catholic Encyclopedia), Kohler (Jewish Encyclopedia), Oesterley (1918) and the New American Bible's introduction agree that a Greek-speaking Jew wrote it, most likely in Alexandria, long after Solomon. Philo, Zerubbabel, Aristobulus and Apollos have all been proposed and set aside (Gigot, 1912). Scholars still differ on whether one writer composed the whole: Eichhorn and Goodrick held one author writing at different times, and Winston (1979) a single author, while Oesterley (1918) leaned to two, pointing to the change in style after chapter 10, the near silence about Wisdom in chapters 11–19, and God acting through Wisdom in the first half and directly in the second. Kohler (Jewish Encyclopedia) saw three independent parts.

audience.to: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria, Egypt, under the last Ptolemies or the first Roman emperors. They lived in a great Greek city full of temples, animal gods and ruler worship, with schools that taught Plato and the Stoics, and some of them were tempted to give up the God of their fathers or had already done so. Formally the book speaks to "you who judge the earth" and to kings (1:1; 6:1–11), and from chapter 11 to God himself, but its real readers were Jews who could read refined Greek.
audience.why: To hold them to the God of Israel when faith cost something. It answers the scoffer's creed that death ends all (2:1–20) with the hope that the righteous live on with God (3:1–9; 5:15). It shows that true wisdom, which the Greeks prized, is God's gift and came to Israel through Solomon. It mocks idols and the worship of rulers (13–15), and retells the Exodus to say that the God who judged Egypt still protects his people (19:22). Knowing this audience explains the book's mix: Greek words for Jewish faith, and the Bible's story told for readers who were again living in Egypt.
views: Goodrick (1913) tied it to the troubles of the Jews of Alexandria under the emperor Caligula (AD 37–41), when Jews were pressed to honor the emperor's image, and dated it soon after (AD 41–44). Grätz too saw allusions to the deification of Caligula (Oesterley; Kohler). Luther had already set it in that crisis: in his preface (1534) he reports that some hold Philo to be its author, recalls that Philo was sent to Caligula to defend the Jews of Alexandria and was not heard, and thinks the book arose from that failure, to frighten the persecutors with God's judgment and comfort the Jews.

Toy and Grimm replied that the book need not come from the middle of a persecution: any Alexandrian Jew knew enough of his people's troubles to write chapters 2–5, and ruler worship goes back to Ptolemy I (Oesterley). The New American Bible's introduction speaks of "a time when they had experienced suffering and oppression," without naming one.

Luther also took the address to kings at its word. He quotes the book's words to tyrants in his German of 6:9 ("Euch Tyrannen gelten meine Rede") and says the great lords who rage against their subjects and the innocent should read it above all ("Sonderlich aber solten es lesen die grossen Hansen").

outline: Love justice, you rulers; God did not make death
The ungodly speak: life is short, so let us enjoy it and crush the righteous man
The souls of the righteous are in God's hand; the childless and the early dead
The judgment: the ungodly see the righteous man and confess too late; God arms himself
Kings, seek wisdom; the steps that lead to a kingdom
Solomon's speech: born like everyone, he prayed and Wisdom came; her nature
Wisdom as bride and teacher of every virtue
Wisdom in history, from Adam to the Exodus
Water from the rock: the first contrast between Egypt and Israel
God's mercy and measured punishment of Egypt and Canaan
Those who did not find the Maker from his works
Idols: the carver, the grieving father, the ruler's image, the potter
Animals and plagues; hail and manna, the food of angels
Darkness on Egypt, light for Israel
The death of the firstborn; the all-powerful word leaps from heaven
The sea and creation made new for God's people

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts Wisdom among the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament, defined as Scripture at Trent (1546), and reads it often at Mass, above all 3:1–9 at funerals and on All Souls' Day. With Augustine, it hears in the plot against the righteous man of chapter 2 a prophecy of Christ's passion.

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Eastern Orthodox churches read Wisdom in their Old Testament from the Septuagint; the Orthodox Church in America, for example, lists three readings from it (3:1–9; 5:15–6:3; 4:7–15) for 9 October 2019. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named it among the genuine parts of Scripture; Philaret's Russian catechism (1839) follows Athanasius in counting 22 books and leaves out Sirach "and certain others" because they are not in the Hebrew.

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place Wisdom among the Apocrypha. Luther praised it as worth reading, Anglicans read it for example of life but not for doctrine (Article VI), and Reformed churches give it no authority (Westminster 1.3). Many still study it as the Jewish background of Paul and Hebrews.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Historical-critical scholars read Wisdom as the work of a Greek-speaking Jew, most likely of Alexandria, written sometime between about 220 BC and AD 44 (the proposals run from Gigot's Ptolemies to Winston's Caligula), who joined the Bible's faith with Greek learning to strengthen Jews under pressure.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: Wisdom is not in the Jewish Bible and was never written in Hebrew, but it is a Jewish book through and through: an early witness to the Jews of Alexandria, to beliefs about the soul and judgment, and to ways of retelling the Exodus that have parallels in rabbinic retellings (Kohler).

sections.h: How to read the Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b:
Read it as poetry. Like Proverbs and the Psalms, it is written in pairs of parallel lines, and this site marks the lines with a slash. Read it as a speech: it begins and ends by talking to someone (rulers, then God), and from chapter 11 on it is a prayer. Read it as a book of contrasts: the ungodly and the righteous, the short life the scoffers see and the life God gives, Egypt and Israel, the idol and the living God.

Remember who counts it as Scripture. Catholic and Orthodox readers have it in their Bibles. For Protestant readers it is among the Apocrypha. Whether it is Scripture is asked once, on the opening page of Proverbs ("Are the Wisdom of Solomon and Sirach ... part of Scripture?"); on this page, "Who wrote it?" asks only whether Solomon wrote it.

sections.h: Greek words for a Hebrew faith
sections.b: The writer knew the Bible in Greek, the Septuagint, and quotes it: the ungodly's "Let's set a trap for the righteous man, because he is a nuisance to us" (2:12) takes up the Greek of Isaiah 3:10, which differs from the Hebrew, and "His heart is ashes" (15:10) comes from the Greek of Isaiah 44:20 (Oesterley). He also wrote some of the finest Greek in the Septuagint, with rare words and long chains of adjectives, such as the twenty-one qualities of Wisdom's spirit (7:22–23). Jerome already heard "Greek eloquence" in it. Yet the thought is Israel's: one God, maker of all, who judges and saves, who chose Israel and gave the law.

sections.h: Plato, the Stoics and the Bible
sections.b:
The book uses the language of Greek thinkers. It speaks of the soul and of incorruption (ἀφθαρσία, 2:23; 6:18–19), says "a perishable body is a weight on the soul" (9:15), says God's hand created the world "out of formless matter" (11:17), lists the four virtues the Greeks taught, self-control, understanding, righteousness and courage (8:7), and calls God's care "providence" (πρόνοια, 14:3; 17:2). Wisdom "spreads through all things and passes through them" (7:24), much as the Stoics spoke of the world's reason.

Readers weigh this in different ways. Gigot (Catholic Encyclopedia) held that the Greek terms are used without their Greek errors: "formless matter" need not mean that matter is eternal, and 8:19–20 can be read without the pre-existence of souls. Kohler (Jewish Encyclopedia) found the book's Wisdom "very close to the Platonic wisdom." Some Protestants used 8:19–20 as a reason to reject the book (Gigot). The chapter pages give the views side by side, with cards at 3:1 and 8:19.

The first half (1–9, or 1–10) is about the righteous and Wisdom; the second (11–19) hardly names Wisdom and speaks straight to God about the Exodus. Toy described the style of the first as "relatively simple and direct," with constant regard to Hebrew parallelism, and the second as "ambitious, grandiloquent, or turgid" (Oesterley). So Oesterley thought of two writers, while Eichhorn and Goodrick held one writer at different times, and Winston (1979) argued for a single author. Kohler (Jewish Encyclopedia) saw three independent parts. Chapter 10, where Wisdom saves the righteous from Adam to Moses, is the hinge either way.

The book never names its author. From 7:1 to 9:18 the speaker is a king who prayed for wisdom and was told to build the Temple, that is, Solomon, and the Greek codices title the book "Wisdom of Solomon." The writers who have asked who wrote it say it was not Solomon. Augustine wrote that "the more learned have no doubt that they are not his," while the church, "especially the Western," had received the book into authority (City of God 17.20). Jerome called it a "falsely ascribed work" and reported that some ancient writers held it to be Philo's. Luther's preface (1534) says it is called Solomon's because it was composed under Solomon's name and person, and that some hold Philo to be its master ("Es solle Philo dieses Buchs Meister sein"). Gigot (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1912) wrote that it is "freely admitted that Solomon is not the writer," quoting Vigouroux that the book was ascribed to him because its author, "through a literary fiction," speaks as the son of David; the New American Bible's introduction names an unknown member of the Jewish community at Alexandria.

What divides the churches is the book's authority, not its author. For the Catholic Church that authority does not rest on Solomon's name: the First Vatican Council taught that the Church holds the books of Scripture sacred and canonical because "they have God as their author" (Dei Filius 2). Whether the book is Scripture is set out side by side on the opening page of Proverbs.

There is no date in the book. The earliest limit is its use of the Greek Bible. The ungodly's words at 2:12 come from the Greek of Isaiah 3:10, "His heart is ashes" (15:10) from the Greek of Isaiah 44:20, and 12:12 from the Greek of Job 9:12, 19 (Oesterley). The Greek of the Prophets existed before 132 BC, as the prologue to Sirach shows. Job belongs to the third and latest part of the Hebrew Bible, whose Greek translation cannot be dated so well, and Oesterley judged that its use suggests "a considerably later date as the earliest possible one, say somewhere about the beginning of the Christian era," though he called neither point conclusive. The latest limit is its use in the New Testament, if Paul and Hebrews knew it. Between those limits scholars have argued from its politics and its thought:

  • Under the Ptolemies. Gigot (1912) thought the writer had in view Ptolemy IV Philopator (221–204 BC) or the king he calls Ptolemy VII Physicon (145–117 BC), kings remembered for harming Jews, and found it "confessedly difficult to decide" between them.
  • Well before Philo. Gregg (1909) argued that it shows no trace of Philo's teaching on the Logos and so was written "a considerable time, perhaps a century, before Philo" began to write. Oesterley answered that this does not carry the book so far back.
  • The first century BC. Kohler (Jewish Encyclopedia) put it about the middle of that century, and the New American Bible's introduction says about fifty years before Christ. Oesterley would "hesitate to date" chapters 1–9 "earlier than about B.C. 50," and of chapters 10–19 would say only that they were written before the middle of the first century AD.
  • Under the Romans. Grätz saw allusions to the deification of Caligula (AD 37–41), and Goodrick dated it AD 41–44, after the persecution of Alexandria's Jews (Oesterley). Winston's commentary (1979) argues that it was written "later than is commonly supposed," during Caligula's reign. Toy and Grimm answered that worship of rulers is far older (Oesterley).

Chapters 11–19 retell Exodus and Numbers, not to add new events but to draw out their meaning. The rule is stated at 11:5: "The very things that punished their enemies / were the things that did them good when they were in need," and at 11:16: "what a person sins with, he is punished with." So Egypt thirsts when the Nile turns to blood while Israel drinks from the rock; Egypt is plagued by animals while Israel is fed quail; hail falls on Egypt while manna falls for Israel; Egypt sits in darkness while Israel has the pillar of fire; Egypt's firstborn die while Israel is spared; Egypt drowns where Israel walks through the sea. The Greek never names Moses, Pharaoh or Egypt: the reader is meant to know the story, and the Plain, as a reader would, writes "the Egyptians" in a few verses where the Greek has only a pronoun (16:3; 18:1–2). Kohler read these chapters as "part of a Passover Haggadah recited in Egypt," and he compares many of their details with rabbinic retellings such as the Mekilta.

No New Testament writer names the book or quotes it as Scripture. But several passages share words and ideas with it, two of them rare. Hebrews calls the Son "the brightness that shines out from God's glory" (Hebrews 1:3) with the word ἀπαύγασμα, which the Septuagint uses only in Wisdom 7:26. Paul's "tent" that weighs us down (2 Corinthians 5:1–4) uses σκῆνος, found in the Septuagint only at 9:15. Romans 1 argues, like Wisdom 13–14, that people could have known the Maker from his works and fell into idols and vice; Romans 9 uses the potter and his clay as 15:7 does; Ephesians 6 arms the believer with "God's armor" (πανοπλία) as 5:17–20 arms God. Scholars weigh these links differently, from Thackeray, who held that Paul "had at one time made a close study" of the book, to those who think both drew on common Jewish teaching. Each link is set out, with its strength, under "Where the Bible uses it."

spec.title: Why the book never says "Solomon"
spec.body: This is Claude's theory. The writer gives every sign that the speaker of chapters 7–9 is Solomon (the prayer for wisdom, the throne, the Temple) and yet never writes his name, and later he names no one at all: not Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Pharaoh or Egypt. That silence may be the point. A reader who knows the story supplies the names, and in doing so learns that the pattern is what matters: anyone who prays as Solomon prayed ("For I am your slave," 9:5) can receive wisdom, and any people God rescues stands where Israel stood. Unnamed figures also suit a book that speaks to many kinds of reader at once.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. canon.summary: The Wisdom of Solomon is in the Old Testament of the Catholic Church and of the Orthodox churches, including the Ethiopian; Catholics call it deuterocanonical, and some Orthodox teachers rank it among the books "to be read." Anglicans and Lutherans place it among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches do not count it as Scripture, and it is not in the Jewish Bible.
accepted_by: Scripture, one of the deuterocanonical books. Augustine defended its authority against those who rejected its witness, saying that for many years it had been read in the church, "from the station of the readers," and heard by all Christians "from bishops downwards" (On the Predestination of the Saints 27), and that earlier teachers such as Cyprian had used it as a divine testimony (28). The list of the Council of Carthage (397), which Hefele held was taken over from the Council of Hippo (393), counts "five books of Solomon"; Augustine names five books sometimes ascribed to Solomon, among them Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus. The Council of Trent (Session 4, 1546) named "Wisdom" among the sacred and canonical books, with an anathema on anyone who does not receive them; the First Vatican Council (1870) confirmed Trent's list, and the Catechism (120) lists "the Wisdom of Solomon." The lectionary reads it on eight Sundays (for example 1:13–15 with 2:23–24, and 2:12, 17–20 in Year B), on All Souls' Day and at funerals (3:1–9; 4:7–14).

In the Old Testament, read in the Greek of the Septuagint. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672), answering Protestant ideas, named "the Wisdom of Solomon" with Judith, Tobit, the Maccabees and Sirach among the "genuine parts of Scripture." Athanasius (367) had placed it among books not in the canon but "appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us," and the Russian catechism of Philaret (1839), counting 22 books, leaves out Sirach "and certain others," unnamed, because "they do not exist in the Hebrew." Its readings are heard in services: the Orthodox Church in America lists 3:1–9, 5:15–6:3 and 4:7–15 among the readings for 9 October 2019, the day of the glorification of St. Tikhon of Moscow.

Scripture, in its 81-book Bible. The church's own list of its 46 Old Testament books has an entry "Metsihafe Tibeb (the books of wisdom)" between Tegsats (Reproof) and Ecclesiastes. R. W. Cowley's study of the Ethiopian canon (1974) explains the books of Solomon as they are understood today: Messalë (Proverbs 1–24), Tägsas (Proverbs 25–31), Tebäb (Wisdom), Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs. In the narrower list, the one printed in the large Ge'ez and Amharic Bibles, Wisdom is among the 14 further books "listed as equally fully canonical."

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles names "the Book of Wisdom" among the other books that the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not apply "to establish any doctrine." The King James Version (1611) printed it among the Apocrypha.

Among the Apocrypha. Luther's preface (1534) says the book has long been in dispute ("lange zeit im zanck gestanden") over whether it belongs among the books of Holy Scripture, but calls it an explanation of the First Commandment ("eine auslegung des ersten gebots") and well worth reading ("wol werd, das mans lese"), above all by rulers.

Not Scripture. The Belgic Confession (1561, article 6) lists "Wisdom" among the apocryphal books the church may read and learn from as far as they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm any point of faith. The Westminster Confession (1646, 1.3) says the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of the Scripture," and are to be used only like "other human writings."

Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) calls the Apocrypha "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture." Many evangelical scholars still read Wisdom closely as background to Paul and Hebrews.

Not Scripture. Wisdom is not in the Hebrew Bible, and Jerome wrote that it was "never among the Hebrews." Josephus counted only 22 books, written from Moses to the reign of Artaxerxes, and said later writings were not held in like authority because the exact succession of prophets had failed (Against Apion 1.38–41). The Jewish Encyclopedia reports that the medieval scholar Nachmanides mentions a Hebrew translation of the book in the preface to his commentary on the Torah.

Widely used, and often quoted as Scripture, with doubts about its rank and author. 1 Clement echoes it twice. At 3:4 it says of envy that through it "death entered into the world," close to Wisdom 2:24. At 27:5 it asks, "Who shall say unto Him, What hast thou done? or who shall resist the might of His strength?" in Lightfoot's translation, close to Wisdom 12:12 and 11:21. Eusebius says Irenaeus quoted it in a book of discourses and used "almost the precise words of the Wisdom of Solomon" (Church History 5.8.8; 5.26). The Muratorian Fragment lists it, oddly, among the New Testament books. Writers who followed the Hebrew count placed it lower: Athanasius among the books "to be read," Rufinus among the "ecclesiastical" books read in the churches but not appealed to "for the confirmation of doctrine," and Jerome among books read "for the strengthening of the people" but not "for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas."

provenance.h: Who wrote it, where and when
provenance.b: A Jew who wrote polished Greek and knew the Greek Bible well, most likely in Alexandria, the capital of Ptolemaic and then Roman Egypt, home of the largest Jewish community outside Judea. The book attacks Egyptian animal worship (12:24; 15:18–19), tells the Exodus as the story of Egypt's judgment, and speaks the language of Alexandrian learning. Its date is unknown: proposals run from the late 200s BC to the 40s AD; the Jewish Encyclopedia and the New American Bible put it about the middle of the first century BC, and Winston in the reign of Caligula (see "When was it written?").

Wisdom books in Israel gathered under Solomon's name because he asked God for wisdom (1 Kings 3:5–15) and was remembered for proverbs and songs (1 Kings 4:32). Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs carry his name in their titles; this book makes him its speaker and so answers, in Greek, the question of what wisdom is. Ancient readers knew this practice: the Muratorian Fragment says friends of Solomon wrote it in his honor, and Jerome called it "falsely ascribed." Writing in the person of a great figure of the past was a known form in that age; it was not meant to deceive a reader who knew the form.

The Jews of Alexandria read their Bible in Greek, and the Christian churches received the Greek Bible from them. The great Christian codices of the 300s and 400s (Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus) contain Wisdom among the books of Solomon, under the title "Wisdom of Solomon." From there it passed into the Latin Bible and the Bibles of other churches, including the Ethiopian. No Hebrew copy has ever been found, and none is expected: the book was written in Greek.

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: Judaism's Bible does not contain it, and it was never written in Hebrew. Josephus limits the authoritative books to 22, written from Moses to Artaxerxes, after which there had not been "an exact succession of prophets" (Against Apion 1.38–41); a Greek book of later date falls outside that count. The Westminster Confession, setting the Apocrypha aside (1.3), cites among its proofs Romans 3:2, that the oracles of God were entrusted to the Jews, and Luke 24:27, 44, where Jesus explains himself from Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms. The argument in its strongest form: the church should receive the books Israel received, and no New Testament writer quotes Wisdom by name or as Scripture. Philaret's Orthodox catechism uses the same reason, that the books "do not exist in the Hebrew," to leave Sirach "and certain others" out of its count.

Jerome (about 398, the date fourthcentury.com gives his preface) called the book "falsely ascribed," said it was never among the Hebrews, and wrote that, as the church reads Judith, Tobit and the Maccabees without receiving them among the canonical Scriptures, so Wisdom and Sirach may be read "for the strengthening of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas." Athanasius (367) set it among the books "to be read" by those preparing to join the church, and Rufinus among the "ecclesiastical" books. These are the roots of Article VI.

Luther's preface notes the long dispute over whether the book belongs among the books of Holy Scripture and the view that Philo wrote it. Many Protestants also objected to its content, above all 8:19–20 ("since I was good, I came into a body without stain"), which they read as teaching that souls exist before birth, a Platonic idea (Gigot reports this objection). The confessions draw the line: the Belgic Confession lets the church read and learn from such books as far as they agree with the canonical books, but not confirm any point of faith from them, and the Westminster Confession allows them no more use than other human writings.

rejected_why.h: How the churches that keep it answer
rejected_why.b: The churches that keep it point to its long use. Augustine answered those who rejected its witness that it had been read in the church for many years, "from the station of the readers," and heard by all Christians "from bishops downwards," and that Cyprian had used it as a divine testimony; 1 Clement echoes it and Irenaeus quoted it. Trent named "Wisdom" among the sacred and canonical books, and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) among the "genuine parts of Scripture." The First Vatican Council taught that the Church holds the books sacred and canonical because "they have God as their author" (Dei Filius 2), so the human author's name is not what gives the book its rank. On the hard verses, Gigot argued that 8:19–20, read in context, "yields a perfectly orthodox sense" and that "formless matter" does not affirm the eternity of matter; the chapter pages give the readings. The question whether it is Scripture is set out side by side on the opening page of Proverbs.

cited_in.b: Hebrews calls the Son "the brightness that shines out from God's glory" (Hebrews 1:3). The Greek word, ἀπαύγασμα (radiance, brightness), appears in the Septuagint only in Wisdom 7:26, where Wisdom is the radiance of eternal light, a mirror of God's working and an image of his goodness; in the New Testament it appears only in Hebrews 1:3. Both the Catholic Encyclopedia and the Jewish Encyclopedia name this parallel. It is one of the strongest verbal links between the book and the New Testament, though Hebrews applies the word to a person, the Son, not to a personified quality.

Paul argues that God's power and divine nature "are visible to the mind in what he has made," so that idolaters have no excuse (Romans 1:20), that people traded God's glory for "an image of mortal man" and of animals (Romans 1:23), and that a long list of vices followed (Romans 1:29–31). Wisdom 13–14 makes the same three moves: the Maker can be seen "by analogy" from the greatness and beauty of what he made (13:5), images of men and animals are carved and worshiped (13:13–14:21), and idolatry is the start of every evil, listed in a long chain (14:12, 22–27). One difference is telling: Wisdom says that for those who worshiped nature "the blame on these people is small" (13:6), then says even they are not to be excused (13:8); Paul leaves no excuse at all. Thackeray (as quoted by Oesterley) held that Paul had studied the book closely; others think both use common Jewish teaching against idols.

"From one lump of clay, does the potter not have the authority to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" (Romans 9:21). Wisdom 15:7 has the potter shaping, "from the same clay," vessels for clean uses and their opposites, with the potter as judge of each one's use. Both use the Greek words for potter (κεραμεύς) and clay (πηλός). Oesterley held the likeness too close to be chance; Goodrick answered that the potter image is common in the Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 29:16; Jeremiah 18:6) and that the two passages make different points, Wisdom about the folly of idol-makers, Paul about God's freedom.

Ephesians tells believers to put on "all of God's armor" (πανοπλία), "with righteousness put on as your breastplate" (Ephesians 6:14). Wisdom 5:17–20 arms God himself: he takes his zeal as full armor (πανοπλία), puts on righteousness as a breastplate, takes holiness as a shield and sharpens his anger into a sword. Both build on Isaiah 59:17, where the LORD puts on righteousness and salvation (compare 1 Thessalonians 5:8). Oesterley judged the likeness between Wisdom and Ephesians too great to be independent; others hold that both expanded Isaiah separately. The direction differs: in Wisdom God wears the armor to judge, in Ephesians God gives it to his people.

Paul speaks of "the earthly house we live in, this tent" and says "we groan under the weight" (2 Corinthians 5:1, 4). Wisdom 9:15 says a perishable body weighs down the soul and the earthly tent (σκῆνος) burdens the mind. The word σκῆνος for the body appears in the Septuagint only in Wisdom 9:15 and in the New Testament only in 2 Corinthians 5:1 and 4, and both passages use the verb "weigh down" (βαρύνω). The thought differs: Wisdom speaks of the soul burdened by the body, while Paul does not want "to be undressed" but to be clothed with a body from God, so that life swallows up what is mortal (2 Corinthians 5:4).

At the cross the leaders mock Jesus: "He has put his trust in God, so God should get him free now, if he takes delight in him. After all, he said, 'I am God's Son'" (Matthew 27:43). The first part follows the Greek of Psalm 22:8 ("let him rescue him, since he wants him"). The last part, the claim to be God's Son, matches the ungodly in Wisdom 2:18: "If the righteous man is God's son, God will take his side / and pull him out of the grip of those who stand against him." The Catholic Encyclopedia lists the parallel, and Augustine wrote that in this book "the passion of Christ is most openly prophesied" (City of God 17.20). Whether Matthew knew Wisdom is disputed: Psalm 22 explains most of the verse, and Wisdom may only show how Jews of the time spoke of a mocked righteous man.

Paul writes that "sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin" (Romans 5:12). Wisdom 2:24 says "death came into the world through the devil's envy." The Greek phrase "entered into the world" is the same. Oesterley read Paul as correcting Wisdom (through a man's sin, not the devil's envy) and so as knowing it; others see only shared Jewish talk about Genesis 3. 1 Clement 3:4 also says of envy that through it "death entered into the world."

"For who has come to know the Lord's mind? Or who has been his adviser?" (Romans 11:34). The Catholic Encyclopedia names Wisdom 9:13 ("what human being can know God's plan?") as a parallel. But Paul's words match the Greek of Isaiah 40:13 almost exactly, so Isaiah is his source; Wisdom shares the theme, not the wording.

John's prologue says everything came to exist through the Word (John 1:3). Solomon's prayer says to God, "by your word you made all things," and that he formed humanity by his wisdom (9:1–2), and the book pictures God's "all-powerful word" leaping from heaven (18:15). John opens with the words of Genesis 1:1, so Genesis is his plain source; Wisdom shows that Jews before him already spoke of God's word and wisdom as his agents in creation. A direct link cannot be shown.

Christ "is the image of the God who cannot be seen" (Colossians 1:15). Wisdom is "an image of his goodness" (7:26), with the same Greek word εἰκών, and was present when God made the world (9:9). The likeness belongs to a wider Jewish way of speaking of Wisdom (Proverbs 8:22–31); the chapter page for Wisdom 7 shows how Christians read the verse in the debates about the Son.

Paul at Athens says God made people "so that they would look for God, in the hope that they might grope for him and find him," and that the Divine is not like gold or silver or stone shaped by human craft (Acts 17:27, 29). Wisdom says the nature-worshipers may only go astray "while they search for God and long to find him" (13:6), and calls those wretched who named as gods gold, silver and useless stone worked by human hands (13:10). The shared words may come from common Jewish preaching to Greeks rather than from the book itself.

The crowd says, "'Bread from heaven he gave them to eat'" (John 6:31), quoting Psalm 78:24 (compare Exodus 16:4). Wisdom 16:20 calls the manna the food of angels and bread sent from heaven, as the Greek of Psalm 78:25 calls it "bread of angels." The link runs through the Psalm; Wisdom shows how Jews of the time praised the manna, a reading that later Christian teachers applied to the Eucharist.

Paul asks whether believers know that God's people will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2). Wisdom 3:8 says the righteous "will judge nations and rule peoples." Oesterley treated this as a common Jewish belief of the time, found also in other books, not as proof that Paul used Wisdom.

Jesus says Sodom will fare better on judgment day than a town that refuses his messengers (Matthew 10:15; Luke 10:12). Wisdom 19:13–15 judges Egypt by its hatred of strangers (μισοξενία) and sets it beside others who would not receive strangers when they came; the Greek names no one, but the comparison recalls Genesis 19. The site's notes on Matthew and Luke read the saying beside it. It shows a Jewish memory of a town that refused guests, not a use of this book.

Jesus speaks of those who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. Isaiah 56:3–5 had promised faithful eunuchs a place in the LORD's house, and Wisdom 3:14 takes that up: the eunuch who has done no lawless deed will be given a share in the Lord's temple. Both depend on Isaiah; nothing shows that Matthew used Wisdom.

Mark's list of the evils that come from the heart and Wisdom 14:25–26, the evils that follow idol worship, share the form of a vice list and some words: murder, theft, deceit (δόλος), adultery and shameless living (ἀσέλγεια). Such lists were common in Greek moral writing and in Jewish teaching; the order differs, and no dependence can be shown.

Paul's list of the works of the flesh is a vice list like Wisdom 14:25–26, and both name shameless living (ἀσέλγεια). The site's note on Galatians 5:19 sets the two side by side as examples of a form common in Hellenistic Judaism, not as a borrowing.

Paul speaks of being enslaved under the elements (στοιχεῖα) of the world. Wisdom 7:17 uses the same word for the working of the elements that God taught Solomon to understand, and 13:2 names fire, wind, air, the stars and water as things people took for gods. That is one of the readings of Paul's phrase; others take it as first lessons or as spirit powers (see the note on Galatians 4:3).

Mary wraps her son in swaddling cloths (ἐσπαργάνωσεν). In Wisdom 7:4 the king says he too was nursed in swaddling cloths (σπαργάνοις), because no king had any other beginning. The shared picture is of an ordinary birth; Luke shows no sign of using the book.

Jesus speaks of Wisdom proved right by her children, and in Luke 11:49 the Wisdom of God sends prophets and apostles. Wisdom 7:27 says that in every generation she passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets. Luke's sayings draw on the Jewish picture of Wisdom as a person that Proverbs 8 and this book share; the exact saying of 11:49 is found in no known book.

Moses and Elijah speak of Jesus' departure (ἔξοδος). Wisdom 3:2 uses the same word for the death of the righteous, whose going was thought a misfortune. The word was a common way to speak of death (compare 2 Peter 1:15); with Moses present it also recalls the Exodus.

Jesus says no one knows who the Son is except the Father. Jewish writers spoke of Wisdom as known fully only by God and present with him when he made the world (Job 28:12–27; Wisdom 9:9–17). The likeness is in the pattern of speech, not in words.

Jesus says much will be asked of the one to whom much was given. Wisdom 6:6 warns kings that the least may be pardoned in mercy, but the mighty will be mightily tested. The thought is the same, the wording different.

Jesus pairs Noah's flood with Lot and Sodom and tells his hearers to remember Lot's wife. Wisdom 10:4–7 also pairs the flood with Lot's rescue from the fire on the five cities, and calls the pillar of salt a monument to an unbelieving soul. The pair belonged to Jewish teaching on judgment (2 Peter 2:5–9 has it too).

Luke's centurion calls Jesus righteous, where Mark has God's Son (Mark 15:39). In Wisdom 2:18 the ungodly test whether the righteous man is God's son. The site's note on Luke 23:47 sets them side by side because the book joins the two titles; Luke does not cite it.

John says God's children were born not of blood (in Greek a plural, bloods). Wisdom 7:2 describes the king formed in the womb, formed in blood from a man's seed, which shows the ancient picture of conception that may explain John's plural. It is background, not a source.

Jesus compares his being lifted up with Moses' bronze snake (Numbers 21:8–9). Wisdom 16:6–7 calls the snake a token of salvation (σύμβολον σωτηρίας) and says that whoever turned to it was saved not by what he saw but by God, the Savior of all. Both read the story as pointing past the snake; John shows no use of the book.

Jesus calls the devil a killer from the beginning. Wisdom 2:24 says that death came into the world through the devil's envy, one of the earliest Jewish texts to tie the devil to Eden. John's saying stands in the same tradition.

Jesus asks for the glory he had with the Father before the world existed. Jewish writers said Wisdom was with God when he made the world (Proverbs 8:22–31; Wisdom 9:9–10). Early Christians applied such language to Jesus; the likeness is in the idea.

Judas fell headlong (πρηνής) and burst open. Wisdom 4:19 says God will burst the ungodly, speechless and headlong (πρηνεῖς). The shared word and picture describe the shameful end of the wicked; Acts does not cite the book.
The believers pray to God as Master (δέσποτα). Wisdom 6:7 calls God the Master of all (ὁ πάντων δεσπότης), and the title is common in Jewish prayers in Greek (Judith 9:12; 2 Maccabees 15:22).

Stephen calls Jesus the Righteous One (also Acts 3:14; 22:14), whom the fathers killed. Wisdom 2:12–20 has the ungodly plot against the righteous man who calls himself God's child and condemn him to a shameful death. The title rests above all on Isaiah 53:11; Wisdom shows the same figure in Jewish use.

Paul says God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance (εἰς μετάνοιαν). Wisdom 11:23 says God overlooks people's sins so that they may repent (εἰς μετάνοιαν), and 15:1 calls God kind and slow to anger (χρηστὸς ... μακρόθυμος), words that Romans 2:4 also uses. The site's notes on Romans 2:1 and 2:4 suggest Paul turns this comfort against a judge who presumes on it; the ideas also stand in Exodus 34:6.

Paul calls on the conscience (συνείδησις) as a witness in Gentiles. The word is rare in the Septuagint: Swete's text has it only in Ecclesiastes 10:20 and Wisdom 17:11, where a guilty conscience torments the wicked. The site's note on Romans 2:15 names the verse as Wisdom 17:10, by another numbering.

Paul's chain from trouble to endurance to tested character to hope has a parallel in Wisdom 3:5–6, where God tested the righteous like gold in a furnace. The picture of testing by fire is common in the Bible (Proverbs 17:3; 1 Peter 1:7).

The objector asks who can resist God's will (τίς ἀνθέστηκεν), and Paul answers that what is formed cannot ask its maker why he made it so (Τί με ἐποίησας). Wisdom 12:12 asks who will say to God, What have you done (Τί ἐποίησας), or who will stand against his judgment (τίς ἀντιστήσεται). Oesterley took 12:12 as a quotation of the Greek of Job 9:12, 19, and Paul's image of the pot and its maker comes from Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9, so the shared words may come from Job and Isaiah rather than from Wisdom. 1 Clement 27:5 uses the same question.

Paul says there is no authority except from God. Wisdom 6:3 tells kings that their power was given them by the Lord, who will examine their works. Jewish teaching had long said rulers are set by God (Daniel 2:21); Wisdom adds the warning to the rulers themselves.

Paul calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Wisdom 7:25 calls Wisdom a vapor rising from God's power and a clean outflow of the Almighty's glory. Paul gives to Christ language that Jewish writers used of Wisdom; how far he has a Wisdom Christology is debated (see the note on 1 Corinthians 1:24).

Paul says all things are through Jesus Christ. Solomon's prayer says God made all things by his word and formed humanity by his wisdom (9:1–2). Paul gives that role to Christ, as John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16 do.

Paul says the grumblers were destroyed by the destroyer (ὁ ὀλοθρευτής). Wisdom 18:25 speaks of the destroyer (ὁ ὀλοθρεύων) who drew back from Israel in the wilderness. Both name the figure of Exodus 12:23; Paul does not need Wisdom for it.

Paul quotes the slogan of eating and drinking because tomorrow we die from the Greek of Isaiah 22:13. Wisdom 2:1–9 puts the same creed in the mouth of the ungodly who think life is short and death the end. Isaiah is Paul's source; Wisdom shows the creed he answers.
Paul calls Christ the image of God (εἰκών). Wisdom 7:26 calls Wisdom an image of God's goodness with the same word. Genesis 1:26–27 is also behind Paul's words; see the entry for Colossians 1:15.

Paul describes the Gentiles' darkened minds and shameless living. Wisdom 13–14 makes the same Jewish case against pagan life: ignorance of God, idols, and the immorality that follows (14:12 calls the idea of idols the beginning of sexual immorality, πορνεία). Romans 1:18–32 has the same pattern.

Christ destroyed the one who holds the power of death, the devil. Wisdom 2:24 says death entered the world through the devil's envy. Hebrews assumes a tie between the devil and death that Wisdom is among the first to state.

Hebrews says God's word is sharper than any two-edged sword. Wisdom 18:15–16 pictures God's all-powerful word leaping from heaven like a warrior with a sharp sword (ξίφος, not Hebrews' μάχαιρα). Both join word and sword, as Isaiah 49:2 does.

James lists the marks of the wisdom from above: pure, peaceable, gentle, full of mercy. Wisdom 7:22–23 lists twenty-one qualities of Wisdom's spirit, holy, unstained and kind to humanity among them. The form, a chain of qualities, is shared; the words mostly are not.

The rich have condemned and murdered the righteous man. In Wisdom 2:10–20 the ungodly plot to oppress the righteous poor man and condemn him to a shameful death. James may mean any righteous poor person, as Wisdom does, or Jesus; the site's note on James 5:6 gives the readings.

Peter calls his body a tent (σκήνωμα) that he must soon put off. Wisdom 9:15 calls the body an earthly tent (σκῆνος) that weighs down the mind. The word differs, but the picture of the body as a tent is the same; compare 2 Corinthians 5:1–4 and Isaiah 38:12.

2 Peter calls Lot righteous (δίκαιον). Wisdom 10:6 says Wisdom rescued a righteous man (δίκαιον) when the ungodly perished and he fled the fire that fell on the five cities. Genesis never uses the word of Lot; Wisdom shows the Jewish tradition 2 Peter follows.

Revelation names the ancient snake as the devil and Satan. The Hebrew Bible never makes that link outright; Wisdom 2:24, which lays death at the devil's envy, is among the first Jewish texts to make it.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Jewish faith in the Greek-speaking world around the time of Jesus, Wisdom is of the first rank: it shows how a learned Jew of Alexandria held to one God, the law and Israel's story while using the words of Plato and the Stoics, and it gives one of the clearest pre-Christian Jewish teachings on the soul's life with God after death. As a text it survived well: written in Greek, it is in the great codices of the 300s and 400s, with only small differences among them. It makes no historical claims of its own beyond the Exodus, which it retells freely, and its use of Solomon's voice is a literary form that ancient readers already recognized. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees with their faith in the one Creator, his justice and mercy and the folly of idols; it goes beyond them in its teaching on immortality and on Wisdom as God's radiance; and in a few verses (8:19–20; 9:15; 11:17) it uses Greek ideas that the churches read in different ways.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Judaism in the time of Jesus: very high
sections.b: Here the churches and scholars agree. The book shows a Greek-speaking Jewish community answering its neighbors: mocking idols and animal gods, contesting ruler worship, claiming that Israel's God gives the wisdom the Greeks sought, and keeping the Exodus at the center. It is one of the clearest Jewish books to speak of the righteous dead at peace with God and of incorruption as God's purpose for humans (2:23; 3:1–9). It explains why New Testament writers could speak of Christ as God's image and radiance and of the body as a tent: those words were already in Jewish use.

Because the book was written in Greek, the copies we have are copies of the original language, not of a translation. Codex Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus (300s–400s AD) all contain it, Codex Ephraemi has parts, and Swete's notes show their differences, mostly of spelling and small words. This site's Plain follows Swete's printed text (Codex Vaticanus), with a variant note wherever it departs or where the other codices or the KJV read differently in meaning.

sections.h: 3. Its claims about itself and history
sections.b: The book claims Solomon's voice, not his name, and ancient readers already took that voice as a literary form (the Muratorian Fragment, Jerome, Augustine). It tells no new history of its own. Its Exodus chapters (11–19) add details to Exodus and Numbers: the Egyptians terrified by phantoms in the darkness (17), creation itself remade so that Israel could cross the sea (19:6–21). These read best as reflection on the story, with parallels in rabbinic retellings (Kohler), not as a separate historical record.

Where it agrees. One God, Creator of all; his justice and patience (11:23–12:2); the folly of idols, told in the words of Isaiah 44 and Psalm 115; Solomon's prayer for wisdom (1 Kings 3); the Exodus as God's judgment and rescue.

Where it goes beyond. It speaks more plainly than the Hebrew Bible of immortality and of the souls of the righteous at peace with God (3:1–9), and of Wisdom as an outflow of God's glory and the radiance of his light (7:25–26). Christians who hold the book as Scripture see here the Old Testament reaching toward the New; Protestants read it as the Jewish background the New Testament drew on.

Where readers find tension. The verses on the good soul entering an undefiled body (8:19–20), the body that weighs down the soul (9:15) and the world made from formless matter (11:17) have been read as Greek ideas at odds with the Bible's teaching on creation and the body, or as poetic language that fits it. Wisdom 2:24 lays death at the devil's envy, where Genesis 3 and Romans 5:12 stress human sin; the two can be read as complementary. The chapter pages give the churches' answers, with cards at 3:1 and 8:19.

how_to_read.b: If you are Catholic or Orthodox, Wisdom is in your Old Testament, and your church reads it at funerals, on saints' days and on Sundays. If you are Protestant, it is not Scripture for you, though Luther called it worth reading and the Anglican tradition reads it for example of life. Either way, it is the best window we have into how Jews in the Greek world thought about death, wisdom and idols in the time around Jesus.

Read 1 Kings 3 before Wisdom 7–9, Isaiah 44:9–20 and Psalm 115 before Wisdom 13–15, Exodus 7–14 before Wisdom 11–19, and Isaiah 52:13–53:12 beside Wisdom 2 and 5. Then read Romans 1, Hebrews 1:1–4 and 2 Corinthians 5:1–10, and judge for yourself how close the New Testament comes to it.

Chapter 2 and 5:3–13 are the ungodly speaking: their creed ("Life is short for us ... let's make the most of the good things around us," 2:1, 6) is what the book rejects, not what it teaches. From 7:1 to 9:18 the speaker is "Solomon." From chapter 11 the writer prays to God. Knowing who speaks keeps you from taking a scoffer's words as the book's own.

When the book speaks of the soul, the body and formless matter, read each passage in its strongest light before deciding: the churches that hold it as Scripture read these lines in a way that fits creation and resurrection, and Protestant critics have read them as Platonism. The notes give both.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "the Wisdom of Solomon, in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants." Say that Solomon is its speaker, not its known author. It is among the most helpful backgrounds for Romans 1, Hebrews 1 and the New Testament's language for Christ as God's image.
